questions.prompt: What is the core mistake in the it'll-get-worse-before-it-gets-better fallacy?
choices: Treating present deterioration like proof of future improvement
Rejecting every difficult transition automatically
Assuming comfort is always a sign of success

explanation.gentle: Yes. The bad stretch is being treated like proof.
explanation.direct: Correct. Temporary worsening is being mistaken for evidence of progress.
explanation.competitive: That is the trap. Pain starts forging its own credentials.

questions.prompt: Why is this fallacy emotionally tempting?
choices: Because struggle can feel meaningful and serious
Because all painful processes lead somewhere better
Because confusion is always evidence of deep learning

explanation.gentle: Right. Difficulty can feel like it must mean something important.
explanation.direct: Correct. Pain and disruption can look like signs of seriousness even when they prove nothing yet.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Once the bill arrives, people want a payoff story.

questions.prompt: Which example best fits this fallacy?
choices: A team treats a chaotic rollout as proof that transformation is working
A team checks whether the rollout is producing better results before expanding it
A student leaves a confusing method after finding no progress data

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chaos is being used like evidence of improvement.
explanation.direct: Correct. A worsening process is being granted authority without proof of mechanism.
explanation.competitive: That is it. The mess is getting credit just for being loud.

questions.prompt: What makes this fallacy dangerous in work and school?
choices: It lets pain and confusion replace evidence about whether progress is real
It prevents people from tolerating any challenge at all
It makes all hard tasks automatically useless

explanation.gentle: Yes. A hard stretch starts doing the work that evidence should do.
explanation.direct: Correct. The mistake is letting discomfort validate a process by itself.
explanation.competitive: Right. The grind starts grading its own performance.

questions.prompt: Why is pain alone weak evidence of progress?
choices: Because something can hurt for reasons other than improvement
Because all discomfort is meaningless
Because progress should always feel easy

explanation.gentle: Right. A process can feel bad because it is failing, not because it is working.
explanation.direct: Correct. Difficulty can accompany progress, but it can also reflect waste, friction, or poor design.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Pain can be real and still be buying nothing.

questions.prompt: What is the practical correction in this chapter?
choices: Ask what mechanism links the present cost to the promised gain
Trust every painful transition a little longer
Avoid all processes that feel difficult at first

explanation.gentle: Yes. The correction is to ask what the pain is actually buying.
explanation.direct: Correct. Mechanism and feedback should connect the current cost to a real later benefit.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. Make the struggle show the receipt.

choices: Present suffering with evidence of future improvement
Comfort with laziness
Feedback with criticism

explanation.gentle: Right. The bad stretch starts looking more informative than it really is.
explanation.direct: Correct. The fallacy mistakes the existence of cost for proof of productive causation.
explanation.competitive: Yes. The pain starts trying to pass as the payoff.

questions.prompt: Why can a confusing class method still be a bad sign rather than a good one?
choices: Because confusion needs evidence that it is turning into understanding
Because all difficult classes are poorly designed
Because challenge has no role in learning

explanation.gentle: Yes. Confusion alone does not prove deeper learning.
explanation.direct: Correct. Without feedback showing real competence, the confusion may simply be unproductive.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. The fog has to turn into skill or it is just fog.

questions.prompt: What is the deepest practical correction in this fallacy?
choices: Force the painful process to compete with mechanism, feedback, and alternative explanations
Assume every rough phase will eventually justify itself
Choose whatever feels easiest instead

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter asks you to test the story behind the struggle.
explanation.direct: Correct. Better judgment rebuilds the causal bridge instead of trusting pain by itself.
explanation.competitive: Right. Strip the hero story away and make the process prove itself.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's threshold question?
choices: What evidence shows that this worsening is actually connected to later improvement?
How much pain am I willing to tolerate?
Should I avoid all hard transitions?

explanation.gentle: Yes. That question stops the bad stretch from proving itself too quickly.
explanation.direct: Correct. It tests whether a real mechanism connects the present cost to a future gain.
explanation.competitive: That is the test. Can the pain prove it is buying the future it keeps promising?
